title: Emergence of Fermi-liquid and BCS physics in overdoped cuprates
claims: In an ideal, disorder-free hole-doped cuprate there is a crossover near optimal doping to an overdoped regime described by weak-coupling BCS theory on a Fermi-liquid normal state, with Tθ >> Tc ≈ |Δ0|/2.

Observed overdoped features that contradict this picture (the superfluid-stiffness boomerang, low-T T-linear resistivity, residual C/T and Drude weight, gaps above Tc) are extrinsic effects of substitutional disorder amplified by the short coherence length.
YBCO, the least disordered cuprate, shows a superfluid stiffness that rises with overdoping, unlike Ca-YBCO and other more disordered cuprates (Fig. 2).
Quantum oscillations with Lifshitz–Kosevich form in overdoped Tl2201 establish a Fermi-liquid ground state in the overdoped regime.

Inverting the BCS gap equation on Bi2212 ARPES data gives a short-range pairing interaction of magnitude consistent with magnetic exchange (J ≈ 0.15 eV) that decreases with doping, so no quantum-critical mode is the prime driver of pairing (Fig. 3).
Cleaner overdoped cuprates should show an exponential Tc tail, Tθ >> Tc, Δ0 ≈ 2kBTc, a mean-field specific-heat jump and a vanishing T-linear resistivity.
summary: This Perspective proposes that a disorder-free overdoped cuprate is a weak-coupling d-wave BCS superconductor built on a Fermi-liquid normal state, and attributes the main contrary observations (stiffness boomerang, T-linear resistivity, residual C/T, gaps above Tc) to dopant disorder amplified by the short coherence length. It supports this with YBCO versus Ca-YBCO superfluid-stiffness data, Tl2201 quantum oscillations and an inversion of the BCS gap equation on Bi2212 ARPES data that yields a short-range pairing interaction of magnetic magnitude, and it lists falsifiable predictions for cleaner samples.
strengths: It gives a clear, testable alternative to two-fluid and quantum-critical scenarios for the overdoped regime, with explicit predictions and a named test platform (pressure-doped YBa2Cu3O7).

It brings together evidence from many techniques and families (quantum oscillations in Tl2201, penetration depth in YBCO and Ca-YBCO, NQR linewidths, STM and ARPES gaps in Bi2212, specific heat in LSCO) under one organizing hypothesis.
The contrast between YBCO, which has no boomerang in Tθ, and Ca-YBCO, which does (Fig. 2), is a striking and well-chosen piece of evidence.

Inverting the gap equation to infer the size and doping dependence of the effective pairing interaction (Fig. 3) is an interesting, reusable idea, and the order-of-magnitude link to the parent-compound exchange is suggestive.

issues.claim: Anomalies are extrinsic, due to disorder
issues.headline: Disorder attribution never tested against an independently measured disorder parameter
issues.issue: Each section shows that a disorder mechanism could produce an anomaly (boomerang, T-linear resistivity, residual C/T and Drude weight, gaps above Tc, linear end of the dome), but none shows that the measured size of the anomaly follows from the measured amount of disorder, so the hypothesis can absorb any discrepancy. Existing tensions are not addressed: Tl2201 and LSCO have comparable T-linear slopes per plane despite different disorder, and homogeneous MBE LSCO films show Tθ ∝ Tc over hundreds of samples.

evidence.quote: argue that features that are inconsistent with this approach can in fact be attributed to the expected effects of material disorder

issues.fix: Either estimate, for one material with a known disorder metric, the expected suppression of Tθ, residual C/T and A1 with the favoured puddle or dirty-d-wave model and compare with experiment, or compile existing data at fixed p across samples and families as a disorder-budget table or figure (Tθ/Tc, A1 per plane, residual γ0/γn, uncondensed Drude fraction against ρ0, Dingle temperature or NQR linewidth). Also state what the puddle mechanism predicts for A1 versus ρ0 and explain why the Swiss-cheese picture applies to the MBE LSCO films of ref. 14.
issues.fix_scoped: We summarize key experimental studies of the low-energy properties of overdoped cuprates, identify properties that are and are not compatible with this proposal — and argue that features that are inconsistent with this approach could plausibly be attributed to the expected effects of material disorder, a hypothesis that remains to be tested quantitatively against independent measures of disorder.

issues.headline: YBCO stiffness rise may come from CuO chains, exceeds clean-limit line
issues.issue: The teal points in Fig. 2 mix λa, λb and √(λaλb), and the CuO chains in YBa2Cu3O7 superconduct and contribute to λb, so the 50% rise of Tθ from p = 0.16 to 0.19 could come from chain filling rather than planar stiffness. Several points near p ≈ 0.18-0.19 lie above the 1 + p line computed with m* = 5 me taken from Tl2201, and the data reach only p ≈ 0.19, the first few percent of the overdoped regime.

evidence.quote: the Ca-doped materials exhibit a clear suppression of the superfluid stiffness with increasing hole doping compared with the Ca-free material

issues.fix: Show the chain-free planar (λa-only) stiffness as its own data set, justify or replace m* for YBCO and explain why points exceed the 1 + p bound, and state plainly the limited doping range tested. If data exist, add other low-disorder overdoped systems (YBCO-248, inner planes of multilayer cuprates) and overdoped Tl2201 and LSCO stiffness on the same Tθ axis.
issues.fix_scoped: In YBa2Cu3Ox, Tθ combining a- and b-axis data, which may include a CuO-chain contribution, rises from p = 0.16, where Tc = 94 K, to p = 0.19, where Tc = 88 K (Figure 2), although this covers only the first few percent of the overdoped regime.

issues.claim: Tl2201 quantum oscillations show Fermi liquid
issues.headline: Tl2201 is both the clean benchmark and shows disorder features, unreconciled
issues.issue: Tl2201 supplies the clean Fermi-liquid evidence (quantum oscillations, m* = 5 me, ħ/τ = 2.4 meV), yet the same family shows T-linear resistivity, strong phase fluctuations, a specific-heat jump only 10% of the residual C/T, and inhomogeneity on a few-hundred-Å scale, all attributed to disorder. It is not shown how a landscape strong enough to leave most specific-heat weight uncondensed still permits coherent cyclotron orbits, and ħ/τ = 2.4 meV is comparable to kBTc ≈ 2.2 meV, so homogeneous pair breaking may already explain the observations.

evidence.quote: There have been several theoretical proposals attempting to reconcile the unambiguous evidence from quantum oscillations for the existence of a Fermi liquid with the observed transport anomalies.
evidence.location: Reconciling results on the Fermi-liquid ground state

issues.fix: Estimate the Dingle damping expected from the hole-density variance the puddle picture requires and compare with the measured damping; estimate ξ0/ℓ relative to the Abrikosov–Gorkov critical value; discuss whether the quantum-oscillation, specific-heat and transport samples are at comparable p and disorder; and, if one sample shows both quantum oscillations and T-linear resistivity, make the puddle reconciliation quantitative for it, including the T-linear term relative to the T² term.
issues.fix_scoped: There have been several theoretical proposals attempting to reconcile the unambiguous evidence from quantum oscillations for the existence of a Fermi liquid with the observed transport anomalies, although whether they are quantitatively consistent with the measured Dingle damping and specific heat of the same Tl2201 samples remains to be established.

issues.headline: Gap-equation inversion depends on an unexamined cutoff; procedure and errors missing
issues.issue: Eq. 7 is inverted with F(ε) = 1, so the integral runs over the full ~1 eV band, although the effective theory is defined below a scale of order J and the analysis is restricted to below ~0.1 eV. The inferred Ṽ ≈ 0.6 eV, the identification J ≈ 0.15 eV and the pronounced decrease of Ṽ used as evidence for magnetic pairing all depend logarithmically on this cutoff, and the inversion procedure and uncertainties are not given.

evidence.quote: the magnitude of the pairing interaction can be determined from an empirical fit to the measured dispersion and the gap function

issues.fix: State whether μ is recomputed at each p, whether t, t′ and t⊥ are fixed with doping, how bilayer bands are averaged, which Δ0 is used, which points the red line is fitted to and how Δ_extrap is computed. Show Ṽ(p) for a range of cutoffs (0.05, 0.1, 0.3 eV, the bandwidth, none) and propagate uncertainties in Δ0, tight-binding parameters and bilayer treatment into error bars on Ṽ and J.
issues.fix_scoped: With no high-energy cutoff (F = 1), the inferred pairing interaction at optimal doping, Ṽ ≈ 0.6 eV, is of the expected magnitude for local exchange interactions, but this value depends logarithmically on the cutoff and should be regarded as an order-of-magnitude estimate.

issues.headline: Load-bearing arguments deferred to missing Supplementary Information and Box 1
issues.issue: The crossover-versus-phase-transition argument, the relation to a quantum critical point at p*, and the distinction between homogeneous dirty-d-wave pair breaking and self-organized granularity are deferred to SI Sections I-III, and Fig. 1 refers to a Box 1, none of which is in the submission. The granularity distinction is the debate on which the extrinsic attribution rests, so the main conclusion cannot be evaluated.

issues.headline: Inversion applied where Δ0 is twice the BCS value
issues.issue: For p ≲ 0.2 the measured Δ0 in Fig. 3 is about twice 2.14 kBTc and the paper says Δ0/kBTc reaches 4 or more near optimal doping, so a weak-coupling inversion there gives a Ṽ of unclear meaning. These points set the slope of the decrease used to argue for magnetic pairing, and the J ≈ 0.15 eV estimate uses the optimal-doping value.

evidence.quote: However, even if only the near-nodal gap [96] is assumed to be the direct consequence of pairing, this ratio grows with underdoping and reaches values in excess of 4.

issues.fix: Restrict the fit to the range where Δ0 ≈ 2.14 kBTc or state how much the J estimate changes, and show both Ṽ inferred from Δ0 and from Tc (or the Tc predicted from the inferred Ṽ next to the measured Tc).
issues.fix_scoped: For the inferred value of Ṽ = 3J̃(1) − 4Ũ(1) = 4J, this corresponds to J ≈ 0.15 eV, in rough agreement [104] with values inferred in undoped antiferromagnet cuprates [105], although at optimal doping the measured Δ0 exceeds 2.14kBTc by about a factor of two, so this estimate lies outside the range where the weak-coupling inversion is self-consistent.

evidence.quote: the same can be said of the Migdal–Eliashberg treatment of conventional superconductors such as Pb, for which the dimensionless strength of the electron–phonon coupling

issues.fix: Explain what small parameter justifies a mean-field treatment at Ṽρ ≈ 1 without retardation, and estimate the strong-coupling corrections to Δ0/kBTc expected at this coupling before using Δ0/kBTc → 2 as evidence of BCS behaviour; these also set how close to 2.14 the ratio should come in the cleanest samples.
issues.fix_scoped: The self-consistency of this analysis can legitimately be questioned, given that we have obtained values of the pairing interaction, Ṽ, that are not small: Ṽρ(EF) ∼ 1 at optimal doping, dropping to Ṽρ(EF) ∼ 0.5 at the highest doping (Figure 3), so the mean-field treatment is at best semi-quantitative and strong-coupling corrections to Δ0/kBTc should be expected.

issues.headline: Abrikosov–Gorkov statements and Eq. 9 conflict with standard dirty d-wave results
issues.issue: If κ ∝ Tc with a fixed prefactor, the 2D ratio Tθ/Tc tends to a constant rather than diverging; standard AG theory for a sign-changing gap gives Tc vanishing as a square root and ρs ∝ Tc², under which homogeneous pair breaking already drives Tθ/Tc down as Tc → 0. With ξ0 only 2-3 lattice constants, kFξ0 is of order a few and prefactors decide the conclusion, which changes the case for needing mesoscopic granularity.

evidence.quote: However, this does not indicate that phase fluctuations become important (and BCS theory therefore inaccurate).
evidence.location: Eq. 9; Effects of disorder on a BCS d-wave superconductor

issues.fix: Give the explicit AG result for κ(Tc) in the d-wave Born and unitary limits, derive Eq. 9 with prefactors and stated assumptions, and show where the observed Tθ/Tc values fall relative to the homogeneous prediction.
issues.fix_scoped: Whether homogeneous Abrikosov–Gorkov pair breaking alone can reach a regime in which Tθ/Tc ≲ 1 depends on order-one prefactors and on the scattering limit, and we do not settle it here.

edit_scoped.before: As far as we know, accessing a regime in which Tθ/Tc ≲ 1 requires something beyond BCS theory.
edit_scoped.after: Whether homogeneous Abrikosov–Gorkov pair breaking alone can reach a regime in which Tθ/Tc ≲ 1 depends on order-one prefactors and on the scattering limit, and we do not settle it here.

issues.headline: d-wave gap shape does not rule out quantum-critical pairing
issues.issue: The paper infers from Δ(k) ≈ Δ0 d(k) that the interaction is nearest-neighbour and that this precludes pairing by a quantum-critical mode. But ξ0 is only 2-3 lattice constants, the gap shape is a Fermi-surface projection, and spin-fluctuation exchange peaked near (π, π) with short correlation lengths also gives gaps dominated by the lowest d-wave harmonic; the authors note that bounds on higher harmonics are lacking.

evidence.quote: This precludes any theory that identifies optimal doping with the point at which the pairing arises primarily from the exchange of any familiar quantum-critical collective mode.

issues.fix: Quote the bound the cited ARPES data (refs 83, 96, 102) impose on the cos 2kx − cos 2ky admixture, translate it into a bound on the interaction range and on the correlation length of any mediating mode, and state how large a harmonic a critical mode would produce; otherwise soften 'precludes' and 'no quantum critical mode is the prime driver' to statements of consistency.
issues.fix_scoped: This is consistent with, but does not by itself exclude, theories in which the pairing arises primarily from the exchange of a quantum-critical collective mode with a short correlation length.

issues.headline: Bi2212 used as clean gap input yet cited as strongly inhomogeneous
issues.issue: Bi2212 is the main source for the BCS-like gap ratio and the Fig. 3 inversion, yet the same material is cited for large gap inhomogeneity, puddles up to 120 K and an ARPES gap persisting 50% above Tc, all attributed to disorder. It is unclear why a spatially averaged ARPES gap there reflects the clean-limit Δ0, and the ARPES-determined p in the most overdoped samples is sensitive to surface doping.

evidence.quote: We focus on the ARPES results on Bi2212, where good tight-binding fits to the electronic dispersion have been obtained and for which the cleanest measurements of the superconducting gap are available.
evidence.location: The nature of the mechanism; Fig. 3

issues.fix: Explain why averaged gaps from a strongly inhomogeneous material are a faithful input to a clean-limit gap equation, or show that the conclusions hold when restricted to dopings where STM gap maps are narrow.

issues.claim: Fermi-liquid ground state in overdoped regime
issues.headline: Direct Fermi-liquid evidence covers only p ≥ 0.27 in Tl2201
issues.issue: The proposal covers the whole regime p > p_opt, but quantum oscillations with LK form exist only in Tl2201 for p ≥ 0.27 (Tc ≤ 26 K). For 0.16 < p < 0.27, where most of the overdoped dome lies and where T-linear resistivity and incoherent transport are reported, the evidence for well-defined quasiparticles is indirect.

evidence.quote: Correspondingly, the normal state, with superconductivity suppressed either by increasing temperature or magnetic field, should be well captured by the usual Fermi-liquid theory of metals.

issues.fix: State the doping range in which the Fermi-liquid ground state is directly established and discuss what evidence exists in the intermediate window (ARPES quasiparticle widths, specific-heat γ, Wiedemann–Franz tests).

issues.headline: Predicted exponential Tc tail and p_max come from an assumed extrapolation
issues.issue: The exponential tail (Eq. 8, Fig. 3 inset) follows from assuming that Ṽ(p) is analytic and crosses zero linearly at p_max, and the sign change near p ≈ 0.31 and the Δ_extrap points come from a straight-line extrapolation beyond the data. The tail shape is an input, not an output.

evidence.quote: Simple fits to the existing data (black and red lines) enable smooth extrapolations to higher values of doping, for which no data exist.

issues.fix: Say explicitly that the tail shape is assumed, give the fit uncertainty in p_max and α, show how the predicted p_max and tail change under other plausible forms of Ṽ(p), and state what observed Tc(p) would falsify the picture.
issues.fix_scoped: Simple linear fits to the existing data (black and red lines) are extrapolated to higher values of doping, for which no data exist; the resulting tail shape is an assumption of this extrapolation rather than an output of the analysis.

issues.headline: Predictions are qualitative and do not discriminate between alternatives
issues.issue: Predictions such as 'should become increasingly rounded' or 'should become increasingly small' are not tied to a disorder scale or numbers, so almost any partial improvement in cleaner samples would count as support. They do not distinguish this picture from two-fluid or quantum-critical scenarios.

evidence.quote: deviations from the predictions of Fermi-liquid theory for the low-energy properties of the normal state, and of BCS mean-field theory for the superconducting state, become less pronounced in overdoped cuprates when disorder is weaker

issues.issue: Hydrostatic pressure or uniaxial strain changes the bandwidth, the chain-plane charge transfer and the c-axis spacing at the same time, so a Tθ(p) or ρ(T) result under pressure cannot be interpreted without an independent measure of p and disorder.
